'''Dorothy Maharam Stone''' (July 1, 1917<ref>{{cite book|last=Gale|first=Thomson|title=American Men & Women of Science: Q-S|year=2003|isbn=0787665290|page=1022}}</ref> – September 27, 2014<ref name="obit">{{Cite web|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/bostonglobe/obituary.aspx?pid=172613269|title=Dorothy Stone Obituary|year=2014|newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]]}}</ref>)
was an American mathematician born in [[Parkersburg, West Virginia]], who made important contributions to [[measure theory]] and became the namesake of [[Maharam's theorem]] and [[Maharam algebra]].<ref>{{cite conference
  | last = Oxtoby
  | first = John C. 
  | title = Biographical note
  | book-title = Measure and Measurable Dynamics, Proceedings of a Conference in Honor of Dorothy Maharam Stone held September 17–19, 1987
  | publisher = [[American Mathematical Society]]
}}</ref>

==Life==
Maharam earned her B.S. degree at [[Carnegie Institute of Technology]] in 1937 and her Ph.D. in 1940 under [[Anna Johnson Pell Wheeler]] from [[Bryn Mawr College]] with a dissertation entitled ''On measure in abstract sets''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=6987}}</ref> Part of her thesis was published in the [[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]]. Then she went on to a postdoc at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]],<ref>{{cite journal |title=News and Notices |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=47 |number=10 |date=December 1940 |pages=721–723 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1940.11991047 }}</ref> where she first met fellow mathematician [[Arthur Harold Stone]]. They married in April 1942.<ref>{{Cite web |title=An Interview with Arthur Stone, by W. W. Comfort |url=http://at.yorku.ca/t/o/p/c/16.htm |access-date=2024-02-21 |website=at.yorku.ca}}</ref>

Stone and Maharam both lectured at various universities in the US and the United Kingdom, including Northeastern University and University of Manchester,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-12-09 |title=Dorothy Maharam Stone - Scholars {{!}} Institute for Advanced Study |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/dorothy-maharam-stone |access-date=2024-02-21 |website=www.ias.edu |language=en}}</ref>  and were faculty at the [[University of Rochester]] for many years. She was an invited speaker at a [[measure theory]] conference at [[Northern Illinois University]] in 1980.<ref>{{cite journal |title=News and Notices |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=87 |number=5 |date=May 1980 |pages=422–423 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1980.11995055 |last1=Haeder |first1=Paul A. }}</ref> Their two children, David and Ellen, both became mathematicians as well.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cohn |first=P. M. |author-link=Paul Cohn |date=September 2002 |title=Arthur Harold Stone (1916–2000) |url=https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1112/S0024609302001091 |journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=34 |issue=5 |pages=613–618 |doi=10.1112/S0024609302001091 |issn=0024-6093|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

She retired in 2001. Her husband, Arthur Stone, died August 6, 2000, and her son, David Stone, died August 27, 2014. She died a month later in [[Brookline, Massachusetts]] and was buried at Kehillath Jacob Cemetery in  [[West Roxbury]].<ref name="obit"/>

==Contributions==
Maharam pioneered the research of [[finitely additive]] measures on integers. [[Maharam's theorem]] about the decomposability of  complete measure spaces plays an important role in the theory of [[Banach space]]s. Maharam published it in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]]'' in 1942.  Another paper of Maharam, in 1947 in the ''[[Annals of Mathematics]]'', introduced [[Maharam algebra]]s, which are complete Boolean algebras with continuous submeasures.

==Recognition==
Maharam was named a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 1976.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/historic|title=Historic Fellows|publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science|access-date=2021-04-21}}</ref>
